### Recommendation

You should unequivocally choose `std::sort` for this task. Implementing a custom QuickSort for production C++ code is generally discouraged unless you have highly specific, constrained requirements that standard library algorithms cannot meet. `std::sort` is part of the C++ Standard Library and is implemented by top-tier compiler engineers (like those from Intel, AMD, or LLVM teams) who optimize it extensively for modern CPU architectures. For sorting 10,000,000 uniformly distributed doubles, `std::sort` will consistently outperform a naive or even moderately optimized custom QuickSort. It provides robust performance guarantees, typically using Introsort (a hybrid of QuickSort, HeapSort, and Insertion Sort), which avoids the worst-case quadratic time complexity inherent in pure QuickSort. Furthermore, relying on the standard library ensures better maintainability, readability, and immediate compatibility with parallel execution policies like `std::execution::par`, allowing you to leverage multi-core processors with minimal code changes, whereas a custom implementation would require significant additional engineering effort to achieve similar concurrent performance.

### Supporting basis

Practical performance considerations favor `std::sort` due to sophisticated low-level optimizations that are difficult to replicate manually. First, template specialization allows the compiler to generate highly optimized machine code for `double` types, often utilizing SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions to compare multiple values simultaneously, significantly accelerating the comparison phase. Second, `std::sort` employs cache-oblivious or cache-aware strategies to minimize memory access latency, a critical bottleneck when handling 10 million elements that exceed L1 and L2 cache sizes. Custom QuickSort implementations often suffer from poor pivot selection, leading to unbalanced partitions and degraded performance, even with random data. In contrast, `std::sort` uses hybrid algorithms like Introsort, switching to HeapSort if recursion depth exceeds limits guaranteeing O(N log N) worst-case performance. Additionally, the standard library implementation is heavily tested across diverse hardware platforms, ensuring consistent behavior. A custom solution likely lacks these hardware-specific tuning knobs and rigorous validation, introducing unnecessary risk of subtle bugs or suboptimal constant factors that accumulate significantly over ten million comparisons.<|im_end|>
